prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if INR is above 1.7, the platelet count is below 100,000, there was recent major surgery, or another guideline-listed contraindication is present.
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or laboratory results in a stroke alert.
Do not delay thrombectomy to observe the response to IV thrombolysis.
Do not start anticoagulation within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis or before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation, and do not bridge with heparin.
Do not discharge on antiplatelet therapy alone for atrial fibrillation-related cardioembolic stroke.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (12:15, 2 hours 47 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (22).

IV thrombolysis: give (2 hours 47 minutes from last known well, no contraindication, not anticoagulated, INR 0.9, glucose 174 mg/dL). Thrombectomy: proceed for the left ICA terminus and M1 occlusion (NIHSS 22, independent before the stroke, ASPECTS 10, within 6 hours); do not wait for the response to thrombolysis.
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg (185/100 on arrival) with IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; after successful recanalization do not target systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Control the ventricular rate of atrial fibrillation (114 to 117 bpm on arrival) with a beta-blocker given intravenously or by nasogastric tube until a swallowing screen is passed, avoiding hypotension.

Repeat troponin and review the ECG; the mild elevation (troponin I 0.07 ng/mL) is most likely demand ischaemia from rapid atrial fibrillation or neurogenic myocardial injury; it does not delay reperfusion.

Start a DOAC for atrial fibrillation (apixaban 5 mg twice daily; CHA2DS2-VASc 5; HAS-BLED 3 for this stroke, age over 65 and aspirin) on day 6 to 7 for this major infarct, once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation; do not bridge with heparin, and stop aspirin when the DOAC starts.
Discuss anticoagulation with him and his wife: his earlier refusal followed a minor fall, and the risk of recurrent cardioembolic stroke outweighs the bleeding risk of a fall.
Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg daily (LDL 139 mg/dL on 40 mg) with an LDL target below 70 mg/dL, for carotid atherosclerosis and diabetes.

key_clinical_evidence: Last known well 12:15, 2 hours 47 minutes before arrival: within the 4.5-hour IV thrombolysis window, and he takes no anticoagulant (INR 0.9).

Global aphasia with right hemiplegia, right facial and sensory loss, right-sided extinction and leftward gaze deviation localise to the dominant left hemisphere, matching the infarct and the occlusion.
NIHSS 22 (LOC questions 2, commands 1, gaze 2, face 2, right arm 4, right leg 3, sensory 1, language 3, dysarthria 2, extinction 2).
Left ICA terminus and M1 occlusion with NIHSS 22 and ASPECTS 10 within 6 hours: thrombectomy is indicated (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 1), with IV thrombolysis first and no wait for its effect.
A normal non-contrast CT under 3 hours does not exclude infarction; the MRI shows DWI restriction without FLAIR change, as expected in the hyperacute window.
Atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc 5) is the mechanism (TOAST cardioembolism); bifurcation plaque under 50% does not meet the large-artery category.
Troponin I 0.07 ng/mL with atrial fibrillation at 114 to 117 bpm: repeat it; it does not delay reperfusion.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Jennings is a 72-year-old right-handed man with a history of atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia who was brought to the emergency department by EMS after his wife found him slumped in his recliner at approximately 14:30 today. She reports that they had eaten lunch together at 12:15 and he was entirely at his baseline at that time, conversant and eating without difficulty with both hands. She went to run errands and returned home at 14:25, at which point she found him leaning to the right in his chair with his right arm hanging limply at his side. He appeared to be trying to speak but could only produce unintelligible sounds. She immediately called 911. EMS arrived at 14:38 and noted left gaze deviation, right facial droop, right-sided hemiplegia, and global aphasia. A prehospital stroke alert was activated. Finger-stick glucose in the field was 168 mg/dL. He was transported emergently to our comprehensive stroke center. On arrival at 15:02, the patient was in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response on the cardiac monitor. He appeared anxious and was making repetitive vocalizations but no recognizable words. There was no reported preceding headache, seizure activity, recent head trauma, or febrile illness. His wife confirms he has not been taking any anticoagulant. She notes he has been generally well recently with no recent hospitalizations or illness. His last known well time is established at 12:15 today, approximately 2 hours and 47 minutes prior to ED arrival.
